titulo: Te mo ii desu ka — ask, and the yes is yours
subtitulo: One opener unlocks the terminal to the pillow — pay, buy, board, sit, top up the phone — because the rule changes with the building
cena: Your bag is on the trolley, three ways into town are signposted, and each of them has a condition you have not been told.
frasePiso: The action in its te-form, then te mo ii desu ka. One opener, and every counter between the plane and the pillow becomes answerable.

clique.desconto: Nobody gave you a different sentence for the machine, the taxi and the desk. You kept one ending and swapped only the action in front of it.
clique.piso: Next time you are unsure whether something is allowed here, you will not guess and hope. You will ask, with the action plus te mo ii desu ka.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: In Japan there is no legal obligation to accept a card, and many small, older or family-run places are cash-only — usually signposted at the door or till. Konbini, chains, department stores, major transport and most hotels do take cards and IC cards such as Suica. Contactless and QR payments (PayPay and similar) spread fast after the government's cashless push, but they have not reached everywhere, so a cash-only ramen counter or shrine stall is normal, not a snub.
fatosDatados.fonte: Sem obrigação legal de aceitar cartão no Japão; muitos estabelecimentos pequenos/antigos são somente-dinheiro, em geral sinalizado. Konbini, redes, lojas de departamento, transporte e maioria dos hotéis aceitam cartão e IC. Expansão do cashless (PayPay etc.) após incentivo governamental, mas não universal.

steps.pt: Between the plane and the bed there are four counters, and each one has its own rule about what you may do there.
The frame: action in te-form, then te mo ii desu ka — may I, then the job. The ending never moves; learn the verb already in te-form.

steps.pt: No business here must take a card; many small places are cash-only. Konbini, chains and transport take cards and IC; yen always works.

aprofundar.titulo: One opener, the whole route into town

secoes.titulo: Te mo ii desu ka plus the te-form
secoes.corpo: Keep te mo ii desu ka and change only the action in front. You learn the verb as a memorised chunk already in its te-form — haratte, suwatte, oite — and never conjugate anything under pressure, which is what makes this the cheapest frame you own. It is deliberately the short te mo ii desu ka and not the longer keigo te mo yoroshii deshou ka: the short form is the one that comes out at a counter.

secoes.corpo: Japan runs heavily on cash, and accepting a card is a business decision, not a legal duty. Small, older and family-run places are often cash-only, usually with a sign, and that is normal rather than a refusal aimed at you. Konbini, chains, department stores, hotels and major transport take cards and IC cards like Suica, and contactless and QR payments have spread fast — but not everywhere. Cash in yen, on the other hand, is always taken.

Between the main airports and the city some routes have a fixed fare you can ask for; otherwise a Japanese taxi runs on the meter. Either way there is no tipping — it is simply not done — and the driver will give a receipt on request. One more thing about the taxi: the rear passenger door is opened and closed by the driver, so you wait for it rather than reaching for the handle.

Whether you can pay by card, bring the case aboard or leave it at the desk varies by company, by building and by hour. A memorised rule gives you one answer. The frame gives you the answer everywhere, including in the places nobody wrote a guide about.

permissao: You do not need a different sentence for the machine, the platform, the cab and the desk. The action, te mo ii desu ka, and a rising tone is a complete request anywhere on that route, and nobody there is grading the phrasing.
espelho: Anyone landing in an unfamiliar airport at home already runs this triage without noticing — money, ticket, bag, somewhere to sit. The only new part is doing it with one ending that never changes.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You reach for the taxi door to open it, and the driver looks put out, or the door swings on its own before you touch it.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: The door is broken, or the driver is being controlling about his cab.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The rear passenger door of a Japanese taxi is operated by the driver and opens and closes automatically. You are not meant to touch it — reaching for the handle is what reads as odd, not waiting for it. It is a fixture of the cab, not a comment on you.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stand back a step, let the door open and close itself, and get in or out without touching it. And do not tip — the fare on the meter or the sign is the whole amount.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The small friction at both ends of the ride disappears, and you stop reading a standard fitting as the driver's mood.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not the front door or the boot, which you may need to handle yourself, and not every private-hire car — the automatic door is a feature of the metered taxi, not of every vehicle you might ride in.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A small restaurant or ticket counter waves your card away and points at a handwritten sign.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They are refusing my card because it is foreign.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: There is no legal duty in Japan to take a card, and many small or older places are cash-only, usually with the condition posted at the door or till. The sign being pointed at is the whole of the explanation — the same thing happens to local customers.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Carry enough yen for the first day, and read the door before you commit to a queue. Konbini and chains will take the card and an IC card; a cash-only ramen counter will not.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stop reading a posted policy as a personal decision, and you stop being caught at the front of a queue with nothing that works.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not for cash in yen, which is always accepted. And the mix is shifting fast toward cards, IC and QR in the cities, so cash-only is a reason to carry a cushion, not to assume cards never work.
